title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Compliance Evidence
author: Ava Martinez
summary: Company-wide security and compliance controls covering RBAC and auth, audit logging, data residency & retention, secure SDLC, incident response procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and risk/exception handling.
body:
Overview

This document consolidates the core controls, operational procedures, and evidence workflows used by Redwood Inference to meet internal security and external compliance obligations. It is intended for engineering, security, product, and compliance stakeholders who own or operate services that process customer data.

Sections covered: RBAC & Authentication, Audit Logging & Monitoring, Data Residency & Retention, Secure SDLC, Incident Response (security), Compliance Evidence Workflows, Risk & Exceptions.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Objective:
- Ensure least-privilege access to systems, services, and data across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Standards and Roles:
- Role definitions (examples):
  - platform-admin: full control over infra projects, only granted to operations SREs and security admins.
  - infra-engineer: deploy and manage infra resources, no access to customer secrets.
  - runtime-operator: manage serving runtime, access to telemetry and metrics, access to model artifacts per onboarding policy.
  - product-engineer: repo and service-level access scoped to owned services.
  - support-agent: read-only access to customer metadata for troubleshooting, must use ephemeral access tokens.

Authentication:
- Primary SSO: Okta. All human access uses SSO with MFA (TOTP + hardware token for privileged roles).
- Service-to-service auth: short-lived mTLS certificates issued by internal CA; services require PID and signed token.
- Secrets: KMS (AWS KMS or customer-managed KMS for Private deployments). No long-lived plaintext secrets in repos.

Policy enforcement and tooling:
- Access requests and reviews must be handled through our Access Management Portal (AMP). All grants expire automatically after a defined TTL unless renewed.
- Quarterly role reviews: owners listed below must attest to role membership.
- Just-in-time (JIT) elevation for emergency operations via vault/AMP with approval logging.

Ownership:
- Policy owner: Security team (Ava Martinez)
- Operational owner: Eng-Infra (team lead: Daniel Park)

2) Audit Logging & Monitoring

Goals:
- Maintain an immutable audit trail for administrative actions, RBAC changes, access grants, and security-relevant events.
- Provide retention and access controls for audit logs per compliance requirements (SOC2, ISO27001, customer contracts).

Logging scope and sources:
- Identity and access events: Okta SSO events, AMP grant requests, role changes.
- Infrastructure control plane: Terraform apply, API gateway admin actions, cluster control-plane events.
- Serving runtime: model load/unload, API key usage, model version rollouts, fallback/routing policy changes.
- Data plane: access to customer storage, data export jobs, backups.

Log collection pipeline:
- Agents forward logs to centralized logging tier (Elastic/Datadog-internal pipeline). Logs are hashed and signed on ingest to provide tamper evidence.
- Audit indices are write-once with access controls; only security and compliance roles have read access by default.

SLOs / Retention:
- Pipeline availability: 99.95% ingestion success for production tenants.
- Log retention: default 1 year for admin/audit logs; 7 years for customer-mandated retention if contract requires.

Access and alerting:
- Alert on suspicious admin behavior: multiple failed SSO attempts followed by elevation, mass policy changes, exfiltration patterns.
- Access to raw audit logs requires approval from Security + Compliance and is recorded.

Example alert thresholds (config table):
| Alert name | Trigger | Owner | Initial severity | Action window |
|------------|---------|-------|------------------|---------------|
| Admin brute-force | 5 failed SSO attempts for admin user within 10m | Security-ops | P1 | 15m |
| Mass role changes | >10 role changes in 5m | Security | P2 | 1h |
| Unusual data export | >100GB export in 1h from backup service | Cloud-ops | P1 | 30m |

3) Data Residency & Retention

Principles:
- Customers choose region(s) for their data. Redwood enforces physical residency constraints in Hosted and Dedicated offerings. Private customers control on-prem footprint.
- Minimum necessary: only store data required for a feature (e.g., short-lived caches excluded).

Region mapping and controls:
- Hosted: region selection at tenant creation (us-west-2, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1). All persistent storage and backups for a tenant are pinned to the chosen region unless the customer explicitly consents to cross-region processing.
- Dedicated: dedicated GPU pools and storage in customer-specified cloud region; encryption keys may be customer-provided.
- Private: data residency is customer's responsibility; Redwood provides deployment playbooks and checks.

Retention policies:
- Default retention: logs/audit events 1 year, model telemetry 180 days, ephemeral KV caches 30 days.
- Customer-configurable retention: customers can request longer retention via contract (evidence recorded in compliance artifacts).
- Automated deletion: retention sweeps run daily; deletion jobs are logged as audit events.

Data deletion procedure (numbered steps):
1. Customer submits deletion request via Console or support ticket (DREQ-<id>).
2. Verify request identity and scope.
3. Schedule deletion window and notify customer.
4. Execute deletion workflows (db purge, S3 object lifecycle, index tombstone).
5. Validate with integrity checks and provide deletion certificate to customer.

Ownership:
- Data residency policy owner: Product Compliance (Priya Kaur).
- Execution owner: Eng-Platform and Eng-Infra.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Software Development Lifecycle)

Goals and coverage:
- Integrate security controls into every phase of development: design, build, test, release, and run.

Required controls by phase:
- Design: threat modeling for all services that handle customer data; record mitigations in design doc.
- Build: enforce dependency scanning (Snyk) and SBOM generation; pipeline fails on critical vulns for prod branches.
- Test: unit/integration tests plus security tests (fuzzing for parsing components, secret scanning).
- Release: pre-deploy security gates (IaC linter, drift checks, signed artifacts).
- Run: runtime protection (WAF rules, Warden policies), runtime signing for model artifacts.

Gating and exceptions:
- Release to production requires a passing security gate. Exceptions must be submitted with risk statement, mitigation, and expiry date; all exceptions are timeboxed to 30 days by default.

Developer guidance (checklist):
- Create/update threat model for service changes.
- Run dependency and container image scans; remediate or document accepted risk.
- Add health and security metrics to service dashboard (auth failures, unusual latency, error budget usage).

Ownership:
- Secure SDLC owner: Research/Applied ML + Security (joint).

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Purpose:
- Provide clear, fast, and auditable steps to contain, investigate, and remediate security incidents affecting confidentiality, integrity, or availability.

Classification:
- P0 (Data exfiltration or active abuse), P1 (service-impacting incidents with potential data exposure), P2 (isolated incidents, low impact).

Key steps (playbook):
1. Detection and Triage: On-call receives alert (PagerDuty). Triage lead assigns severity and incident lead.
2. Containment: Apply short-lived mitigations (revoking tokens, network rules, rolling back offending change).
3. Evidence preservation: Preserve logs, take VM snapshots, record chain-of-custody for artifacts.
4. Investigation: Security and SRE run root cause analysis; collect timeline and affected assets.
5. Communication: Notify stakeholders per comms plan (internal, legal, affected customers). Regulatory notifications follow legal timelines.
6. Remediation and Recovery: Patch, harden configs, rotate keys, and verify system health.
7. Post-incident review: Produce postmortem with timeline, root cause, mitigations, and follow-up actions (owner + due date).

Pre-approved emergency measures:
- Security may revoke tenant API keys for a tenant-scope incident. Revocations must be logged and communicated.

Evidence handling rules:
- Evidence must be stored in designated S3 bucket (access-limited) and indexed in the incident-tracker ticket. Exported evidence is hashed and access-granted for a minimal set of investigators.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Objective:
- Provide reproducible, auditable evidence packages for external audits (SOC2, ISO27001), internal reviews, and customer inquiries.

Evidence types and owners:
- Controls evidence: policy documents, attestation logs (owner: Security).
- Operational evidence: runbooks, shift logs, incident postmortems (owner: Eng-SRE).
- Technical evidence: configuration snapshots, access logs, deployment manifests, SBOMs (owner: Eng-Infra / Eng-Platform).

Standard evidence package contents (for auditor):
- Control matrix with mapped evidence IDs.
- Relevant logs (timeboxed) and integrity proofs (hashes).
- Attestations from owners with dates.

Workflow (numbered):
1. Audit kickoff and scoping: Compliance owner defines scope and timeframe.
2. Evidence collection: Teams collect artifacts into the Evidence Portal (EP).
3. Review and redaction: Security reviews artifacts for sensitive customer data; redact as required.
4. Packaging and notarization: EP bundles artifacts, computes integrity hashes, and timestamps package.
5. Delivery and tracking: Compliance uploads package to auditor portal and records receipt.

Retention and access:
- Compliance packages and audit reports are retained per legal requirements (min 7 years for regulated accounts). Access requires Compliance + Security approval.

7) Risk and Exceptions

Risk acceptance model:
- Low/Medium/High risk levels with documented mitigations and owners. High risks require executive-level approval and a documented mitigation timeline.

Exception process (short):
1. Submit exception request (form includes risk description, compensating controls, duration).
2. Security reviews and assigns risk level.
3. Approval route: Medium risk -> Security + Product; High risk -> Security + Legal + CTO.
4. Timebox and mitigation tracking; periodic re-review until closed.

Example: Temporary exception to allow legacy auth for migration: must include a migration plan, monitoring, and automatic expiry within 14 days.

  - write: deployment
